title: Adaptive Sealing in Protruding LVOT Calcification During TAVR: A 4-Patient Case Series.
authors: Ahmed M Salem; Karan Rao; Samuel Norman; Noman Ali; Michael S Cunnington; Daniel Blackman; Christopher J Malkin
abstract:
Protruding left ventricular outflow tract calcification represents a high-risk anatomical feature for transcatheter aortic valve replacement, predisposing to paravalvular regurgitation (PVR), annular injury, and conduction disturbance.
We present 4 patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis and protruding left ventricular outflow tract calcific nodules treated with the Navitor self-expanding valve system. Despite uniformly hostile landing-zone anatomy, procedural success was achieved in all cases. Residual PVR ranged from trivial to mild-to-moderate, with no patient developing moderate-or-greater PVR. All patients demonstrated hemodynamic improvement and early symptomatic benefit.
Calcific morphology and nodule orientation, rather than calcium burden alone, may be key determinants of PVR following Navitor implantation in hostile landing-zone anatomy. These findings are hypothesis-generating; the observed pattern of adaptive cuff sealing requires verification in larger, preferably comparative studies before conclusions regarding device-specific sealing mechanisms can be drawn.

title: [Sudden cardiac death and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy : risk assessment and indications for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator].
authors: Amaury Masson; Orianne de la Brassinne Bonardeaux; Nils de Marneffe; Vincenzo Miraglia; Caroline Piette; Patrizio Lancellotti
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a myocardial disease characterized by left ventricular hypertrophy without abnormal loading conditions. Despite significant advances in management, HCM remains a major cause of sudden cardiac death, particularly in young individuals. Prevention relies on accurate arrhythmic risk stratification and the selective implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs). This article reviews current indications for primary prevention ICD implantation in sarcomeric HCM based on the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines and compares them with the more integrative approach proposed by the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA).

title: Temporal Trends in Hospitalization and Interventions for Aortic Stenosis in Canada, 2012-2024.
authors: Maria Servito; Denis Qeska; Suleman Aktaa; Philippe Pibarot; Jessica Forcillo; David Messika-Zeitoun; Janine Eckstein; Ellen Ross; Kendra MacFarlane; Seema Nagpal; Harindra C Wijeysundera
abstract:
Given the paradigm shift from surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) to transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), we examined the temporal trends in AS hospitalization and treatment across Canada.
Data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information Discharge Abstract Database were used for a population-based cross-sectional study of inpatients between April 1, 2012, and March 31, 2024. We estimated national and provincial rates and reported the annual changes in hospitalization for AS, SAVR, and TAVI. Rates were expressed as episodes/procedures per million, and stratified by age group, sex, and urban-vs-rural residence.
Between 2012 and 2024, hospitalizations for AS increased from 259.8 to 362.4 per million. Rates of SAVR declined from 104.4 to 66.5 per million, whereas rates of TAVI rose from 19.0 to 136.9 per million. The average annual per-million increases in AS hospitalizations were highest in Prince Edward Island (25.0), Nova Scotia (22.9), and Newfoundland and Labrador (21.3), particularly among individuals ≥ 80 years of age. The rates of SAVR declined, as the uptake of TAVI increased, with the shift mostly evident in those 60-79 years of age. Rates of TAVI were higher in men than in women, whereas AS hospitalizations were higher in rural than in urban areas.
Not unexpectedly there has been a dramatic shift from SAVR to TAVI observed, with an overall improvement in access to care. Nevertheless, sex-related and geographic disparities persist, highlighting the need for a coordinated national effort to ensure equitable access to AS management.

title: Acute Severe Aortic Regurgitation Immediately After Cardiopulmonary Bypass Initiation in a Patient With a Bicuspid Aortic Valve.
authors: Takumi Yamamoto; Keisuke Sumii
abstract: Antegrade cardioplegia delivery during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is standard practice in cardiac surgery, but it carries a risk of perfusion failure and acute myocardial distension in the presence of aortic regurgitation (AR). In patients with a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), acute exacerbation of AR can occur immediately after initiating CPB. An 80-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve (Sievers classification type 1: L/R fusion), severe aortic stenosis, mild AR, and an ascending aortic aneurysm underwent elective aortic valve replacement and ascending aortic replacement. Immediately after starting CPB and entering ventricular fibrillation (VF), the patient developed sudden, severe AR (vena contracta: 10 mm). This caused rapid left ventricular (LV) dilation and subsequent dislodgement of the LV vent cannula into the left atrium. Real-time transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) promptly identified both the severe AR and the cannula displacement. Following aortic cross-clamping, antegrade cardioplegia failed due to massive regurgitant volume overload into the LV. Prophylactically placed retrograde cardioplegia via the coronary sinus was immediately initiated, successfully achieving rapid cardiac arrest. The planned surgical procedures were completed successfully without further complications, and the patient was discharged in good condition on postoperative day 11. In this patient, the acute exacerbation of AR was likely driven by two key factors: first, a rapid elevation in the transvalvular pressure gradient following CPB onset and VF; and second, the unmasking of latent coaptation failure, stemming from BAV asymmetry and calcification, due to the loss of myocardial tone during VF. Real-time TEE monitoring and prophylactic placement of a retrograde cardioplegia cannula are critical for rapid diagnosis, troubleshooting, and ensuring effective myocardial protection.

title: Lipoprotein(a) Inhibition: Current Evidence, Therapeutic Landscape, and Future Directions.
authors: Pierre Sabouret; Domenico Mario Giamundo; Joanna Popiolek-Kalisz; Luigi Spadafora; Marco Bernardi; Elad Asher; Mamas A Mamas; Dan Atar; Giuseppe Andò
abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, apolipoprotein B-containing lipoprotein that contributes to cardiovascular risk through atherogenic, proinflammatory, and potentially antifibrinolytic mechanisms. Genetic, epidemiological, and mechanistic evidence supports a causal role for elevated Lp(a) in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve disease. In contrast, associations with other cardiovascular phenotypes are less consistent. Since circulating concentrations are largely inherited and only modestly affected by lifestyle measures and conventional lipid-lowering therapies, Lp(a) represents an important component of residual cardiovascular risk. This review summarizes the structural, genetic, and pathogenic characteristics of Lp(a), examines the strength of evidence across coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, calcific aortic valve disease, and heart failure, and discusses measurement, clinical interpretation, and potential biomarkers. The therapeutic landscape has expanded rapidly. Antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNA agents substantially suppress hepatic apolipoprotein(a) synthesis, oral small-molecule inhibitors prevent Lp(a) particle assembly, and in vivo gene-editing strategies aim to provide highly durable reductions. Early-phase trials have demonstrated marked lowering of circulating Lp(a); however, most were not designed to assess cardiovascular outcomes, so direct comparisons among agents are limited by differences in study populations, assays, dosing schedules, and follow-up. Ongoing cardiovascular outcome trials will determine whether selective Lp(a) lowering reduces clinical events and which patients are most likely to benefit. Until these results are available, Lp(a) measurement can refine risk stratification and support intensive management of modifiable risk factors, whereas biomarker reduction alone should not be equated with proven clinical benefit.

title: Inflammation After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation: Mechanisms, Risk Stratification, and Therapeutic Implications.
authors: Mihail Celeski; Michele Marchetta; Emanuele Sammartini; Antonio Sorropago; Mattia Basile; Matteo Morello; Carmine Salzillo; Marco Bernardi; Pasquale Mollo; Francisco José Romeo; Arturo Cesaro; Michele Golino
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) elicits a sterile inflammatory response that is almost universal, yet highly heterogeneous in both magnitude and clinical impact. Initiated by endothelial injury, ischemia-reperfusion, and residual bioprosthetic immunogenicity, peri-procedural inflammation converges on activation of the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and downstream interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-6 signaling, leading to increased C-reactive protein levels. This response is further modulated by patient susceptibility, procedural complexity, and device-specific characteristics. While a controlled response promotes tissue repair and healing, exaggerated activation, which manifests as systemic inflammatory response syndrome in up to two-thirds of patients, has been consistently associated with higher mortality, conduction disturbances, new-onset atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury (AKI), and subclinical leaflet thrombosis. Emerging evidence also implicates gut microbiome-derived metabolites and xenoantigen-driven adaptive immunity as additional contributors to the overall inflammatory burden. Serial biomarker assessment, including C-reactive protein trajectories, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and novel composite indices such as the neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio, combined with multimodality imaging, allows increasingly refined risk stratification. However, no anti-inflammatory therapy is currently established for routine use after TAVI. Colchicine has shown proof-of-concept signals, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors have demonstrated clinical benefit with pleiotropic anti-inflammatory properties, and lessons from IL-1 and IL-6 inhibition trials in ischemic heart disease provide a translational roadmap. This narrative review synthesizes the epidemiology, mechanisms, clinical consequences, and assessment of peri-TAVI inflammation. Moreover, this review proposes a pragmatic inflammatory subphenotyping framework that integrates baseline risk, procedural exposure, and biomarker kinetics. Such a framework may help bridge the gap between observational associations and precision-based therapeutic strategies, shifting peri-TAVI inflammation from a prognostic marker to a modifiable determinant of outcome.

title: Single-Stage Computed Tomography Angiography, Percutaneous Coronary Intervention, and Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in an Octogenarian With Femoral Neck Fracture, Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction, and Severe Aortic Stenosis: A Case Report and Literature Review of Multidisciplinary Approaches.
authors: Ming Zhang; Xietian Pan; Lina Yang; Yang Mu; Bo Jiang; Tao Chen; Jing Wang; Lin Wang; Jiayue Li; Jing Liu; Zhuo Zhang; Changfu Liu
abstract: Geriatric femoral neck fractures are associated with high mortality. Early surgery within 48 hours improves survival, whereas delayed arthroplasty is associated with a 41% increase in mortality. Multimorbidity in this population often prolongs preoperative optimization, thereby exacerbating perioperative risk. Current evidence indicates that 5%-10% of patients with hip fractures have concomitant severe aortic stenosis (AS), which independently increases the risk of anesthesia-related complications. Perioperative acute myocardial infarction further increases mortality risk, making cardiac management a critical challenge. The advent of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized care paradigms. Nonetheless, this situation requires multidisciplinary consensus on optimizing the fracture-to-surgery interval, antithrombotic bridging strategies, and concomitant coronary revascularization. Here, we present a case of single-stage aorta-coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and TAVR in an octogenarian with femoral neck fracture, severe AS, and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). This pioneering case is accompanied by a systematic review of contemporary management strategies.

title: A Propensity-Matched Analysis of Pre Versus Concomitant Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement With Frailty-Related High-Risk Features.
authors: Avery Love; Duc-Hieu Bui; Shahman Shahab; Avinav Sanjel; Chandler O'Leary; Hani Jneid; Aiham Albaeni
abstract:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is frequently performed in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR); however, the optimal timing of PCI remains uncertain, particularly in patients with frailty-related high-risk features. Evidence comparing pre-TAVR versus concomitant PCI strategies in this vulnerable population is limited.
We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network to identify patients with frailty-related high-risk features undergoing TAVR with either pre-TAVR PCI (3 months to 2 weeks before TAVR) or concomitant PCI (same day as TAVR). Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using demographics, comorbidities, frailty-related features, and antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. The primary outcome was a 90-day composite including all-cause mortality, acute kidney injury, bleeding requiring transfusion, gastrointestinal bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome, and ischemic stroke. Secondary outcomes included the composite outcome at 30 days and 1 year, as well as individual components.
After propensity score matching, 361 patients were included in each group with adequate baseline balance. The primary 90-day composite outcome occurred in 27.4% of patients undergoing pre-TAVR PCI and 29.4% undergoing concomitant PCI (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.85-1.35; p=0.56). At 30 days, the composite outcome occurred in 21.9% and 24.4% of patients, respectively (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.85-1.45; p=0.43). At 1 year, the composite outcome occurred in 37.1% of the pre-TAVR PCI group and 38.5% of the concomitant PCI group (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.86-1.25; p=0.70). No significant differences were observed in all-cause mortality at any time point.
Among patients with frailty-related high-risk features undergoing TAVR, pre-TAVR PCI and concomitant PCI were associated with similar short- and longer-term clinical outcomes. No significant differences were observed in the 90-day composite outcome or all-cause mortality. These findings support an individualized approach to PCI timing in frail, high-risk patients.

title: Associations of Mild or Trace Valvular Abnormalities With Cardiac Remodeling in Older Adults: The ARIC Study.
authors: Yumin Gao; Jonathan Rubin; Susan Cheng; Lena Mathews; Ajay J Kirtane; Ron C Hoogeveen; Christie M Ballantyne; Elizabeth Selvin; Martin B Leon; Josef Coresh; Scott D Solomon; Amil M Shah; Kunihiro Matsushita
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract:
The impact of mild/trace valvular abnormalities on cardiac remodeling is not well understood, despite their association with poor cardiovascular outcomes.
Using data from 4684 participants in the ARIC (Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities) Study (2011-2013), aged 66 to 90 years, we examined cross-sectional associations of mild/trace valvular abnormalities (aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, and mitral regurgitation) with cardiac parameters using multivariable linear regression models. Cardiac parameters included cardiac structure (eg, left ventricular mass index), systolic function (eg, ejection fraction), diastolic function, and biomarkers (eg, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T).
The prevalence was 4.3% for mild aortic stenosis, 10.9% for mild/trace aortic regurgitation, and 44.7% for mild/trace mitral regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation showed the most consistent associations with cardiac measures (left ventricular mass index 5.48 g/m2 [95% CI, 4.38-6.57 g/m2]; ejection fraction -1.92% [95% CI, -2.29% to -1.54%]; high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T 0.08 log ng/L [95% CI, 0.05-0.12 log ng/L]). Aortic stenosis was associated with impaired ventricular filling (Ratio of early transmitral flow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular velocity (E/e') lateral ratio 2.00 [95% CI, 1.48-2.53]) and elevated biomarkers (high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T 0.17 ng/L [95% CI, 0.09-0.25 ng/L]), whereas aortic regurgitation was associated with worsened cardiac structure (left ventricular mass index 3.52 [95% CI, 1.76-5.28] g/m2) and systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction -1.54% [95% CI, -2.14% to -0.94%]). A dose-response relationship was also observed between the number of total abnormalities and all cardiac parameters examined.
Mild/trace mitral regurgitation was most consistently associated with all cardiac parameters examined. Aortic stenosis was associated with elevated E/e' lateral ratio and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T, whereas aortic regurgitation was associated with worsening in cardiac structure and ejection fraction. Our study supports the possibility of pathophysiological contributions of these mild/trace valvular abnormalities.

title: Impact of Continuous Baseline and Discharge Blood Pressure on Outcomes After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authors: Thorald Stolte; Jakob Johannes Reichl; Felix Goetzinger; Max Wagener; Ketina Arslani; Anke von Peter; Rahel Berger; Christoph Kaiser; Michael Böhm; Lucas Lauder; Felix Mahfoud; Thomas Nestelberger
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract:
Evidence linking pre- and post-transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) blood pressure (BP) with cardiovascular outcomes is scarce. This study investigated the associations of pre- and post-TAVI BP and their changes as a continuous variable with cardiovascular outcomes.
Patients undergoing TAVI at a tertiary university hospital between 2011 and 2025 with office BP available before and after TAVI were included. The primary outcome was a composite of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) at 1 year. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models incorporating restricted cubic splines for continuous variables were fitted.
Among 1191 patients, BP remained relatively stable from pre-TAVI to 1-year follow-up. Both discharge systolic BP and absolute changes therein from pre- to post-TAVI were significantly associated with MACE at 1 year (P<0.001 for both), whereas baseline systolic BP showed no significant association. BP values <115 mm Hg or >143 mm Hg were associated with a higher risk of MACE 1 year after TAVI. A decrease in systolic BP of -5 to -25 mm Hg was also associated with a lower risk of MACE compared with no change.
While BP remains generally stable in the year following TAVI, both very low and high systolic BP at discharge were associated with higher 1-year MACE. Furthermore, moderate decreases in systolic BP from baseline to discharge appear to be protective. These findings highlight the potential prognostic value of BP optimization during TAVI follow-up and support the role of BP measurements as a clinically translatable, independently associated with long-term outcomes after TAVI.

title: Enhanced recovery after surgery turnkey order set for periprocedural care of the patient undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
authors: Daniel T Engelman; Gorav Ailawadi; Mark J Russo; Keith B Allen; Pinak B Shah; Molly Szerlip; Adnan K Chhatriwalla; Patrick M Wieruszewski; Subhasis Chatterjee; ERAS Cardiac Working Group∗; ERAS Cardiac Working Group
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement is now a leading treatment for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis across the risk spectrum. The choice between transcatheter and surgical aortic valve replacement remains a shared decision, particularly for patients aged 65 to 80 years. Despite extensive device-level randomized evidence and procedural standardization, periprocedural care pathways remain variable across programs. This turnkey order set integrates contemporary guidelines and consensus documents into a practical order set for the periprocedural care of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
Subject matter experts translated existing peer-reviewed society guidelines, expert consensus documents, and randomized trial evidence, identified through a structured PICO-framed (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) literature review, into a sample turnkey order set. Orders derived from consistent Class I or IIa (or equivalent) recommendations across referenced documents appear in the order set in bold type. Orders that were inconsistently Class I or IIa, Class IIb, or supported by peer-reviewed evidence appear in italic type.
Preprocedural care centers on interdisciplinary Heart Team evaluation, frailty and cognition assessment, baseline conduction risk stratification, anemia and iron deficiency screening, structured antithrombotic and endocrine medication management, and weight-based antibiotic prophylaxis. Intraprocedural care prioritizes ultrasound-guided femoral access, procedural sedation when feasible, normothermia, contrast minimization, and balanced procedural anticoagulation. Postprocedural care emphasizes telemetry-guided conduction monitoring, single antiplatelet therapy in patients without an indication for oral anticoagulation, oral anticoagulation alone in those with an existing indication, and early mobilization. Standardized discharge criteria target next-day discharge in appropriately selected transfemoral patients.
Comprehensive periprocedural pathways for transcatheter aortic valve replacement have been demonstrated to shorten length of stay without compromising safety. This turnkey order set translates contemporary guideline recommendations into actionable orders to facilitate standardized adoption of best practices across programs. The composite pathway has not been prospectively validated.

title: Outcomes, survival, mortality, and major adverse events in aortic valve replacement surgeries in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Victory Bassey Effiom; Victor Oluwafemi Femi-Lawal; Atharv Vivek Oak; Oluwasegun John Oyesola; Fatma Kamal Ahmed; Samuel Ghislain Junior Fodop; Michael James Anayo; Achanga Bill-Smith Anyinkeng; Jonas Paul Ibekwe; Kolawole Victor Olalekan; Samuel Mesfin Girma; Daniel Brabi; Ahmet Kilic
abstract:
Aortic valve replacement (AVR) is the definitive treatment for severe aortic valve disease, yet outcome data from Africa remain scarce. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed survival, mortality, and major adverse events after AVR across Africa.
Adhering to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for studies reporting AVR outcomes in African populations, covering randomized trials, cohort studies, case series, and case reports. Subgroup analyses were conducted by AVR modality: surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), minimally invasive surgery (MICS), and transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Study quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2 and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Outcomes included survival, mortality, echocardiographic improvements, and valve- or procedure-related complications.
Of 2547 studies screened, 21 studies involving 1303 patients across 6 African countries were included; 15 (71.4%) studies were from Egypt. Mean age was 60.4 years; 43.3% were female. Aortic stenosis (70.4%) and regurgitation (64.0%) predominated. Modalities included SAVR (45.1%), minimally invasive surgery (27.8%), and transcatheter aortic valve implantation (27.1%). Technical success rate was high (97.5%-100%). Complications included arrhythmias (16.0%), postoperative bleeding (15.0%), paravalvular leak (5.0%), pacemaker requirement (6.0%), stroke (5.0%), and myocardial infarction (3.0%). Reoperation rate was 4.4%. Thirty-day mortality was 5.0% (95% CI. 3.1%-8.1%), with 1-year and 5-year survival of 93.2% and 91.0%, respectively.
AVR outcomes in Africa show favorable success and survival rate although below optimal benchmarks despite resource constraints. However, results are not generalizable continent-wide, given the heavy geographic skew. Complications including arrhythmias and postoperative bleeding necessitate enhanced perioperative protocols.

title: Human Epididymis Protein 4 in Cardiovascular Disease: A Fibrosis-Driven Mediator of Tissue Remodeling and Inter-Organ Communication.
authors: Shinsuke Hanatani; Masahiro Yamamoto; Fumihiko Ogata; Yuki Okuno; Satoshi Araki; Yuichiro Arima; Eiichiro Yamamoto; Yasuhiro Izumiya; Kenichi Tsujita
abstract: Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), originally identified as a tumor biomarker, has emerged as a regulator of tissue remodeling, with roles that extend beyond oncology. Recent findings suggest that HE4 is involved in extracellular matrix turnover, immune system modulation, and maintenance of epithelial balance, indicating its complex role in fibrosis and tissue remodeling. In cardiovascular diseases, the circulating HE4 level is consistently associated with disease severity, myocardial fibrosis, and adverse clinical outcomes in conditions such as heart failure, aortic stenosis, and ischemic heart disease, suggesting its role as a marker of fibrosis-driven remodeling in diverse cardiovascular conditions. Mechanistically, HE4 influences fibrosis via protease inhibition, fibroblast activation, and immune signaling pathways, and may function as a mediator of inter-organ communication. In particular, its strong association with renal dysfunction and expression in injured kidney tissues supports its role in cardiorenal interactions. Recent findings suggest that HE4 plays a role in systemic remodeling processes that extend beyond heart function, including those associated with pulmonary vascular disease. Collectively, these insights propose a conceptual framework in which HE4 acts as a context-dependent regulator of tissue remodeling, integrating structural, immune, and inter-organ communication pathways. This perspective positions HE4 as a biomarker and a mechanistically relevant mediator of disease progression, with potential implications for risk stratification and therapeutic targeting in cardiovascular disease.

title: ASXL1- Mutant Clonal Hematopoiesis is Associated with Calcific Aortic Valve Disease and Promotes Valvular Calcification In Vitro.
authors: Aeron M Small; Liying Xue; Shinsuke Itoh; Cesar De Jeronimo Diaz; Yuto Nakamura; Niekbachsh Mohammadnia; Huajun Liao; Yota Maekawa; Linke Li; Sasha A Singh; Taku Kasai; Luisa Weiss; Mesbah Uddin; Art Schuermans; Spencer Flynn; Elby MacKenzie; James C Engert; George Thanassoulis; Peter Libby; Amil M Shah; Christie M Ballantyne; Pradeep Natarajan; Trevor P Fidler; Elena Aikawa; Michael C Honigberg
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract:
Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is a common valvular heart condition and has no effective medical therapy. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), characterized by the acquisition of somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells which provides a selection advantage, has been associated with incident aortic stenosis (AS), particularly when driven by TET2 mutations.
We evaluated the association of CHIP and gene-specific CHIP subtypes with AS in the UK Biobank (UKB) and with aortic valve hemodynamics in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study to prioritize gene driver mutations for mechanistic study. We then generated human ASXL1 -mutant THP-1 derived macrophage like cells and evaluated the ability of THP-1 conditioned media to promote a calcific response in human valvular interstitial cells (VICs). We additionally performed mass spectrometry proteomics to characterize the ASXL1- mutant THP-1 macrophage secretome. Therapeutically relevant inflammatory pathways were inhibited with anakinra (interleukin [IL]-1) or tocilizumab (IL-6).
Among 449,109 individuals in the UKB with whole exome sequencing, large CHIP clones and non- DNMT3A CHIP subtypes (e.g., TET2 , ASXL1 , and JAK2 CHIP) were independently associated with risk of incident AS. Among 1,963 individuals in ARIC with CHIP sequencing and echocardiographic data, only ASXL1 CHIP was associated with worse aortic valve hemodynamics. In vitro, ASXL1 -mutant human THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells had increased AIM2 inflammasome activation. THP-1 media promoted VIC calcification, which was accelerated in ASXL1 mutant macrophages. Proteomic profiling identified inflammatory proteins linked to valvular calcification. Accelerated VIC calcification was reduced by IL-1 inhibition by anakinra or IL-6 inhibition by tocilizumab.
Integrating human cohort data with experimental evidence using ASXL1 -mutant human macrophage-like cells and human valve cells, these findings identify ASXL1 -mutant CHIP as a distinct inflammatory subtype associated with valvular calcification and support IL-1 and IL-6 signaling as candidate therapeutic pathways for future investigation in CAVD.

title: Lipoprotein(a)-dependent cardiovascular risk in different populations: are thresholds the same?
authors: Brett S Mansfield; Frederick J Raal; Petri T Kovanen; Alpo Vuorio
abstract:
Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and aortic stenosis. Large prospective cohort studies together with Mendelian Randomization studies have established its role in cardiovascular risk which has led to the introduction of screening and the development of Lp(a)-lowering therapies. However, interpretation of Lp(a) results in clinical practice remains a challenge, particularly across populations with significantly different baseline levels.
Lp(a) levels vary according to ancestry. People of African ancestry having the highest median Lp(a) levels, followed by people from South Asia, East Asia and Europe, respectively. However, despite these differences, current Lp(a) risk thresholds are derived from populations of predominantly European ancestry and broadly applied across underrepresented population groups.Available evidence from multi-ancestry cohort studies have shown that while proportional risk for ASCVD may be similar across ancestries, the absolute risk associated with specific thresholds may differ. The application of a universal threshold may lead to over-classification of risk in some populations, resulting in unnecessary edicalization and strain on healthcare systems. Conversely, some populations may be under-classified by a universal threshold potentially resulting in avoidable ASCVD events.
This commentary explores the epidemiological, biological and methodological factors underlying variability in Lp(a) levels and their association with ASCVD across populations. We discuss the advantages and limitations of applying ancestry-specific Lp(a) risk thresholds. Lp(a) measurements in clinical practice should be interpreted in within a broader clinical and population context rather than in isolation.

title: Artificial Intelligence Echocardiographic Interpretation in the Emergency Department: Agreement, Interpretation Yield and Reporting Scope.
authors: Vijay Manivel; Michael Hession; Behzad Mirmiran; Patrick Feeny; Nadi Pandithage; Nasim Erfani; Riaz Humayun; Steven Beatty
abstract:
To assess the agreement between artificial intelligence (AI) interpretation and expert emergency physician sonologist review of echocardiograms performed in the Emergency Department (ED).
Retrospective multicentre agreement study in four Australian EDs. A total of 195 echocardiograms (2016-2023) underwent three-stage adjudicated human expert review. Human reports were compared with us2.ai reports. Agreement across 10 validated parameters was reported as percentage exact match with 95% confidence intervals and kappa under two pre-specified tiers: Guideline Compliant (GC; ASE/EACVI multi-view criteria) and Pragmatic (PR; any available measurement). Reference standard reliability was quantified.
Pooled agreement was 76% at both tiers (GC n = 875; PR n = 1323); AI returned an interpretation in 46% of evaluations at GC and 70% at PR. Four structural parameters reached 78%-87%: right atrial size 87% (κ = 0.62), right ventricular (RV) contractility 83% (κ = 0.42), left ventricular (LV) size 83% (κ = 0.52) and RV size 78% (κ = 0.37). Binary LV systolic agreement was 79% GC and 83% PR. Expert reviewers agreed on 85% of interpretations. Pericardial effusion, aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis, present in 7%-20% of patients, are not reported in the current us2.ai algorithm.
AI agreed with expert review in about three-quarters of evaluations but provided a guideline-compliant interpretation in less than half; a pragmatic approach raised yield to 70% at the same agreement. The AI withheld classifications that experts could reach; its validated scope covers only part of what ED echocardiography must address, and reports did not mark unassessed parameters. This study reports agreement, not accuracy. For now, human expert review of AI reports is required.

title: Large-scale prospective evaluation of co-folding across hundreds of Mac1-ligand complexes and three virtual screens.
authors: Jongbin Kim; Galen J Correy; Brendan W Hall; Moira M Rachman; Olivier Mailhot; Takaya Togo; Ryan L Gonciarz; Priyadarshini Jaishankar; R Jeffrey Neitz; Eric R Hantz; Yagmur U Doruk; Maisie G V Stevens; Morgan E Diolaiti; Rashad Reid; Saumya Gopalkrishnan; Nevan J Krogan; Adam R Renslo; Alan Ashworth; Brian K Shoichet; James S Fraser
abstract: Accurate prediction of ligand-bound protein complexes and ranking them by affinity are central problems in drug discovery. While deep-learning co-folding methods can help address these challenges, their evaluation has been hampered by the difficulties in assessing independence from training data and insufficiently large test sets. Here, we test the ability of co-folding methods to predict the structures of 551 ligands, 489 of which are of sufficient quality for evaluation, bound to the SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain (Mac1) that were determined after the training cutoff dates. AlphaFold3 (AF3), Boltz-2, and Chai-1 each reproduced >50% of the Mac1 ligand poses to better than 2 Å root-mean-square deviation of experiment. Despite the potential for co-folding to describe protein conformational changes that stabilize ligand binding, we did not find that common conformational rearrangements, including peptide flip and a large loop opening, were recapitulated by the co-folding prediction. For AF3 and Chai-1, ligand pose prediction confidence weakly, but significantly, tracked experimental potency, while DOCK3.7 energies were only weakly correlated. Boltz-2 affinity predictions showed the strongest correlation with measured potency and, after calibration, achieved lower mean absolute error than a baseline predictor. We next assessed whether co-folding scores could rescore docking hit lists to distinguish true ligands from non-binders among hundreds of molecules prospectively experimentally tested against AmpC β-lactamase, the dopamine D4, and the σ2 receptors. AF3 ligand pose confidence values did not separate true ligands from high-scoring false positives as effectively as docking scores or Boltz-2 affinity predictions did. Taken together, the modest, but independent correlations of docking score and co-folding confidence or affinity suggest that integrating physics-based and deep-learning approaches may help with hit prioritization and subsequent optimization in structure-based ligand discovery.

title: AI-enabled nystagmus analysis in vestibular assessment: Current evidence and future directions.
authors: Reza Hoseinabadi
journal: Journal of vestibular research : equilibrium & orientation
abstract: Vestibular disorders are common, heterogeneous, and diagnostically challenging. Nystagmus is an important sign in vestibular assessment, but its interpretation can depend on clinician expertise and recording quality. This structured narrative review mapped current evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled nystagmus and eye-movement signal analysis in vestibular assessment, focusing on study characteristics, input data, AI tasks, model architectures, validation approaches, performance metrics, explainability, and clinical applicability. A structured PubMed search identified human studies that developed, validated, or evaluated machine-learning, deep-learning, or related computational methods for nystagmus analysis or vestibular diagnostic support. Fifteen studies were included, most published from 2021 onwards. The evidence was dominated by technical and early-stage model-development studies using VNG/VOG recordings, other eye-movement recordings, or derived features such as pupil trajectories, optical-flow maps, eye and head traces, and slow-phase velocity measures. Applications included nystagmus detection, pupil tracking and signal extraction, pattern or direction classification, quantification or localisation, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo-related diagnostic classification. Deep-learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks and CNN-recurrent hybrid models, were commonly used. However, validation was mainly internal, performance reporting was heterogeneous, explainability was limited, and prospective workflow evaluation or routine clinical implementation was uncommon. AI-enabled nystagmus analysis shows promising clinical potential, particularly for VNG/VOG-based assessment and BPPV-related decision support. Translation into routine practice will require multicentre patient-level external validation, transparent reporting, interpretable outputs, standardised performance metrics, and prospective evaluation in real clinical pathways.

title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence-based and pathologist scoring of murine bile duct hyperplasia.
authors: Ingeborg M Langohr; Dev Kumar Das; Dayananda Siddappa; Nathan Pate; Kuldeep Gautam; Sanjit Jha; Rajesh Ugalmugle; Tijo Thomas; Uttara Joshi; Srinivas Rao; Dinesh S Bangari
abstract: Bile duct hyperplasia in rodents, caused by chemical cytotoxicity, bile flow interference, or aging, is traditionally assessed through time-consuming microscopic examination by pathologists. We developed a deep learning-based, artificial intelligence (AI) model for quick and accurate assessment of bile duct hyperplasia in mice. The study utilized 127 hematoxylin and eosin-stained, mouse liver whole-slide images (WSIs) digitized using Aperio scanners. A segmentation algorithm with a U-Net architecture and an EfficientNet backbone was trained on 1165 areas from 35 WSIs to identify and quantify bile ducts, measure their area percentage using a supervised method, and categorize them into grades 0 to 4 using an unsupervised method. The model was validated on 24 WSIs and tested on 68 WSIs, all independently scored by 3 veterinary pathologists using consensus criteria. The segmentation model achieved Dice scores of 91.75% in training and 85.88% in validation. Testing revealed high sensitivity (95%), specificity (97%), and Dice score (95.45%), indicating robust model accuracy. Model-predicted grades showed strong correlation (r2s = 0.86) with pathologists' consensus scores. This AI-driven approach has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of bile duct hyperplasia assessments in rodent studies, paving the way for more standardized, objective, and high-throughput histological evaluations in preclinical research.

title: Time-Resolved Physically Unclonable Functions Enabled by Solvent-Free Scalable Boron-Based Ultralong Phosphorescent Systems for Machine-Learning-Resilient Optical Encryption.
authors: Changsong Xu; Daxiang Shi; Guoyi Pan; Ru-Jia Wang; Jiankang Qin; Jin Peng; Peng Chen; Yingjuan Sun; Wenjing Lin; Wen-Cheng Chen; Xiaofeng Lin; Dingshan Yu; Guobin Yi
abstract: Anti-counterfeiting technologies are increasingly challenged by advances in imaging and machine learning, exposing the fundamental limitations of conventional static optical security systems. Here, a time-resolved physically unclonable function (TR-PUF) system is established, transforming optical authentication from static pattern recognition to high-dimensional temporal encoding. Central to this approach, boron-based room-temperature phosphorescent (RTP) materials are developed via covalent coupling with coumarin derivatives using a solvent-free strategy that is readily scalable to kilogram-level production, exhibiting a maximum phosphorescence lifetime of over 2 s, an ultralong afterglow visible for up to 30 s, and color-tunable emission. The formation of rigid B-O-C linkages spatially isolates emissive centers, suppressing energy transfer and preserving temporally independent decay channels-an essential prerequisite for high-entropy time-resolved encoding. Randomly embedding these multi-emissive RTP units into a polymer matrix forms a complex encryption structure that enables a dual-entropy encoding mechanism with both spectral and temporal dimensions, generating dynamic time keys for authentication. Moreover, we propose a matched time-gated authentication framework that achieves >99% identification accuracy within 1.2 s while exhibiting resistance against the tested generative machine-learning attacks. This work proposes a practical materials platform and a time-gated authentication strategy, offering a scalable technological path for the development of dynamic optical encryption tags.

title: Toward "Obesityomics": Domain-Specific Omics in Precision Obesity Medicine with a Brief AI Perspective.
authors: Nadia Abu Samra; Sara G I Suliman; Mohammed Al-Hadad; Dorret I Boomsma; Fadwa Alhantoobi; Maithah Alsamahi; Haneen Abufarajallah; Alia Al Tikriti; Zeyar Aung; Selena Richards; Abdulrahim Sajini; Mira Mousa; Fatima Sulaiman; Wael Osman
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract:
Obesity's global rise has outpaced the effectiveness of "one-size-fits-all" prevention and treatment strategies. The promise of precision medicine lies in addressing the etiological and biological diversity of obesity and transforming it into actionable endotypes.
In a narrative review, we analyze "obesityomics," looking at the contributions each omics layer makes to understanding and managing obesity. The areas we evaluate are genomics (heritability, polygenic risk, and monogenic forms), epigenomics (development and environment imprinting), transcriptomics (tissue-specific programs of adipose, liver, muscle, and hypothalamus), proteomics (signaling networks and adipokines), metabolomics and lipidomics (fuel partitioning, lipotoxicity, and metabolic inflection points), and microbiome science (metabolites, host-microbe interactions, and microbial ecology). Our domain-by-domain (single-omics) approach demonstrates how disease taxonomy, causal pathways, and biomarkers can be refined and targeted therapeutically.
We argue that "obesityomics" is a pragmatic approach to aligning omics modalities to the right questions at the right time, not a wholesale merger of datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning and deep learning-should be used in conjunction with quality control, feature selection, modest data integration, and obesity intervention prediction. Among the key challenges in managing sensitive multilayer data are harmonization, standardization, reproducibility, equitable representation, and governance. The translation priorities include prospective studies related to patient-centered outcomes, biomarker panels that are clinic-ready, interoperability standards, and cost-effectiveness evaluations.
The review maps concrete steps to assist people with obesity in making better choices by identifying what each omics domain excels at and introducing a brief AI perspective.

title: "Engineering Sense": Donald Hebb, Nathaniel Rochester, and the Origins of Deep Learning.
authors: Yvan Prkachin
journal: Journal of the history of ideas
abstract: This paper examines the origins of the concept of "deep learning," and traces it to its origins in the ideas of the psychologist Donald Olding Hebb. In the 1930s, Hebb formulated a theory of brain function that was meant to explain the surprising intelligence scores of brain surgery patients. This paper then traces how Hebb's cell assembly theory found its way into the earliest attempts by the IBM engineer Nathanial Rochester to engineer a learning computer in the 1950s. Finally, I examined the legacy of this encounter between neurophysiology and engineering for modern artificial intelligence and neural networking systems.

title: Deep Doubly Debiased Longitudinal Effect Estimation with ICE G-Computation.
authors: Wenxin Chen; Weishen Pan; Kyra Gan; Fei Wang
journal: KDD : proceedings. International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining
abstract: Estimating longitudinal treatment effects is essential for sequential decision-making but is challenging due to treatment-confounder feedback. While Iterative Conditional Expectation (ICE) G-computation offers a principled approach, its recursive structure suffers from error propagation, corrupting the learned outcome regression models. We propose D 3 -Net, a framework that mitigates error propagation in ICE training and then applies a robust final correction. First, to interrupt error propagation during learning, we train the ICE sequence using Sequential Doubly Robust (SDR) pseudo-outcomes, which provide bias-corrected targets for each regression. Second, we employ a multi-task transformer with a covariate simulator head for auxiliary supervision, regularizing representation learning, and a target network to stabilize training dynamics. For the final estimate, we discard the SDR correction and instead use the uncorrected nuisance models to perform Longitudinal Targeted Minimum Loss-Based Estimation (LTMLE) on the original outcomes. This second-stage, targeted debiasing ensures robustness and optimal finite-sample properties. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our model,  D 3   -Net, robustly reduces bias and variance across different horizons, counterfactuals, and time-varying confoundings, compared to existing state-of-the-art ICE-based estimators.

title: Integrated computation-guided thermostabilization of the fungal sweet protein Honey Truffle Sweetener.
authors: Zhikuan Wang; Wen Wang; Feifei Zhu; Yutian Zhang; Yirui Li; Zhiqi Zhu; Ziwan Lu; Ang Huang; Mingjia Yu; Si Liu
abstract: Thermostability limits the use of sweet proteins as sugar substitutes in thermally processed foods. Here, we report an integrated computation-guided workflow for thermostabilizing Honey Truffle Sweetener (HTS), a recently identified fungal sweet protein with low intrinsic stability. We determined the HTS crystal structure and used it to guide subsequent computational analyses. Rosetta and ThermoMPNN evaluated candidate substitutions from complementary physics-based and deep-learning-based perspectives, and the selected single-mutant library was experimentally characterized. The resulting melting-temperature data were then used to develop SMRC-Net, which combines mutation-centered features from the ESM2 protein language model with molecular dynamics-derived structural descriptors to support mutation prioritization. Repeated nested cross-validation supported quantitative Tm prediction within the HTS scaffold, while prospective testing showed 9/10 directional agreement in a small, computationally selected variant set. Validated substitutions were then assembled stepwise in small modules, followed by the introduction of an engineered disulfide bond. The final variant, FM, had a melting temperature of 82.1 °C, 27.5 °C higher than that of wild-type HTS. Untreated FM retained sweetness, while separate heat- and pH-treatment assays showed retained solubility and largely preserved secondary-structure profiles. Sweetness after these treatments was not evaluated. Molecular dynamics analyses indicated that FM was not uniformly rigidified but instead exhibited localized flexibility redistribution and a more consolidated conformational ensemble. This work provides a practical computation-guided framework for protein thermostabilization, with potential applicability to other compact proteins.

title: Research Progress on Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Diabetic Foot Ulcers.
authors: Jinxia Du; Xiaoli Liu; Guihui Wu; Yin Huang; Yan Zhang; Xiang Long; Xiaoyi Yang; Yan Zhou
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: As a typical chronic complication of diabetes, the management of diabetic foot ulcers has long faced multiple challenges, including the highly subjective nature of wound assessment, patients'limited capacity for self-care at home, and the difficulty in predicting healing outcomes. The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) technology offers new approaches to addressing these challenges. Based on recent domestic and international literature, this paper systematically reviews the research progress of artificial intelligence in the care of diabetic foot ulcers, focusing on four key dimensions: intelligent wound assessment (eg deep learning-based image analysis models achieving an F1 score of 93.1% for infection identification and 92.8% accuracy for area assessment), patient self-health management (eg mobile health applications and wearable monitoring devices), the development and application of smart dressings (eg responsive biomaterials and sensor integration), and the prediction of healing trends (eg machine learning prediction models, with support vector machines achieving 85.3% accuracy and an AUC of 0.922 in predicting complete DFU healing). It summarizes key technological achievements and the current status of clinical translation, provides an in-depth analysis of existing shortcomings (including insufficient algorithm generalizability, lack of prospective clinical validation, and absence of data standardization), and outlines future development directions (encompassing multimodal integration, explainable artificial intelligence, and implementation science research), with the aim of offering guidance for the further application of artificial intelligence technology in the field of chronic wound care.

title: Prediction of patient-specific quality assurance for volumetric modulated arc therapy using machine log files.
authors: Yuhan Fan; Jiawen Shang; Peng Huang; Zhihui Hu; Ke Zhang; Xin Xie; Zhiqiang Liu; Hui Yan; Yuan Tian
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Deep learning (DL) models have been used for predicting gamma passing rates (GPRs) of patient specific quality assurance (PSQA) in volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT). As the model input mostly from planning parameters and dose distribution, the effect of motion precision of the treatment machine has frequently been ignored. In this study,the most recent motion precision of multi-leaf collimator (MLC) leaves was estimated by their records in machine log file and used jointly with the beam intensity map to predict GPRs of VMAT PSQA.
The input of the DL model consists of two parts: the MLC positional error map which was estimated from machine log file and the beam intensity map which was obtained from the treatment plan. A UNet++ model was trained to predict the GPR of VMAT PSQA. The effect of feature maps and time intervals in estimating MLC leaf positional error maps on the prediction accuracy was evaluated. In addition, the proposed model was compared with two competing DL models (ResNet and SE-Net) and a classic regression model. The prediction error was quantified by mean absolute errors (MAEs) under two clinical accepted criteria (3%-3 mm and 3%-2 mm). Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) between measured and predicted GPR was also assessed.
The model with the inputs of beam intensity and MLC leaf positional error maps achieved the best performance among all combinations with various input feature maps. The MAEs predicted by the proposed model with MLC leaf positional error map obtained from 5 days' records were 0.90 for 3%-3 mm criterion and 1.74 for 3%-2 mm criterion, whereas those predicted by the proposed model with MLC leaf positional error map obtained from 1 day's record were 1.01 for 3%-3 mm criterion and 1.85 for 3%-2 mm criterion. The proposed model achieved the smaller MAEs (1.01 for 3%-3 mm criterion and 1.85 for 3%-2 mm criterion) than the other two competing models: ResNet (2.85 for 3%-3 mm criterion and 2.83 for 3%-2 mm criterion) and SE-Net (3.53 for 3%-3 mm criterion and 4.55 for 3%-2 mm criterion).
The proposed model that combines beam intensity map and MLC leaf positional error map exhibited a better prediction performance for GPRs of VMAT PSQA. It would be advantageous to include more motion precision information of treatment machine into DL models for high-performance prediction of VMAT PSQA.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology.
authors: Elif Agüloğlu Bali; Yasemin Çakır-Kıymaz; İrem Akdemir; Eda Alp; Feyza Nur Akçin Balan; Merve Büyükkörük; Ravi Kumar Chaudhary; Güle Çınar; Daniele Roberto Giacobbe; Ezgi Gülten; Taliha Karakök; Murat Hakan Kır; Oliver Nolte; Ahmet Kağan Özdemir; Özlem Güler; Eren Öztürk; İbrahim Yıldız; Gökmen Zararsız; Önder Ergönül
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI's emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight.

title: SentiAgent: An agentic LLM framework for context-aware and explainable sentiment analysis.
authors: Uma Yadav; Bhakti Thakre; Sumedha Chokhandre
abstract: Sentiment analysis has become a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) due to the rapid growth of user-generated content across social media, e-commerce, healthcare, education, and customer feedback platforms. Despite the success of transformer-based models and Large Language Models (LLMs), existing approaches often struggle with contextual ambiguity, implicit sentiment, sarcasm, commonsense reasoning, and limited explainability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes SentiAgent, a novel Agentic LLM framework for context-aware and explainable sentiment analysis. The framework employs multiple autonomous agents that collaboratively perform contextual understanding, external knowledge integration, sentiment reasoning, and explanation generation. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets-SST-2, IMDB Reviews, Sentiment140, and Amazon Product Reviews-demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. SentiAgent achieved 97.43% accuracy, 97.18% precision, 96.95% recall, 97.06% F1-score, and 0.99 AUC, consistently outperforming conventional machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based, and standalone LLM models. Ablation studies further validate the contribution of each autonomous agent, while qualitative analyses highlight the framework's ability to produce transparent and interpretable sentiment predictions. The proposed framework provides a scalable and trustworthy solution for next-generation explainable sentiment analysis.•Introduces SentiAgent, a collaborative Agentic LLM framework for context-aware and explainable sentiment analysis.•Combines contextual understanding, external commonsense knowledge, and autonomous reasoning to improve sentiment prediction and interpretability.•Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and transparency over existing approaches.

title: Single-view echocardiography-based deep learning for pulmonary hypertension detection: a multi-level supervised and explainable approach.
authors: Qiumeng Xi; Hebin Liu; Xinpeng Dai; Jiayi He; Qizhi Xu; Yidan Li
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Early identification of pulmonary hypertension (PH), particularly mild disease, remains challenging. We aimed to develop and validate a deep learning (DL) model for noninvasive PH screening using single-view transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), without reliance on Doppler measurements.
In this retrospective study, apical four-chamber (A4C) TTE cine loops were collected between January 2023 and June 2025. A total of 144 patients with PH confirmed by right heart catheterization (RHC), 17 RHC-confirmed non-PH patients, and 95 non-PH controls defined by TTE under strict inclusion criteria were included. An additional temporally independent validation cohort of 40 RHC-confirmed subjects was enrolled between December 2025 and May 2026. Multiple DL architectures were evaluated for detecting PH. Model performance was assessed at both sample and patient levels using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and specificity.
A total of 256 patients with 318 TTE examinations were included for model development and independent validation, and an additional 40 RHC-confirmed subjects with 40 TTE examinations were included for temporal validation. The multi-level supervised model achieved the best performance among the evaluated architectures, with a patient-level AUROC of 1.000 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.998-1.000], sensitivity of 0.954, and specificity of 1.000 in the independent validation cohort. In the temporal validation cohort, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.932 (95% CI: 0.843-0.992), with sensitivity of 0.875, specificity of 0.813, and accuracy of 0.850. In an analysis of 50 RHC-confirmed subjects, the DL model achieved an AUROC of 0.937 (95% CI: 0.865-0.987) for distinguishing mild PH from non-PH, with sensitivity of 0.857 and specificity of 0.864, compared with AUROCs of 0.607-0.825 for conventional echocardiographic parameters.
We developed an interpretable DL framework based on single-view A4C echocardiography for noninvasive PH assessment. The model showed promising performance, including preserved sensitivity for mild PH. Further multicenter prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Ultrasound-based deep learning radiomics with explainable machine learning for predicting benign and malignant thyroid nodules in lymphocytic thyroiditis: a multicenter study.
authors: Ji Zhou; Wenwu Lu; Wei Wei; Ziyi Liu; Wang Zhou; Wei Peng; Wenbo Ding; Xin Wu; Chaoxue Zhang
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Thyroid nodules (TNs) with lymphocytic thyroiditis (LT) complicate ultrasound (US) assessment, and few prediction models have been validated in this population. The aim of this study is to develop and validate a US-based deep learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) model for predicting malignancy in TNs coexisting with LT.
This multicenter hybrid study enrolled 640 patients with pathologically confirmed TNs and concomitant LT. The cohort comprised a training set from Anhui Medical University First Affiliated Hospital (Jixi Road Campus), Anhui Medical University First Affiliated Hospital (High-tech Campus), and Affiliated Hospital of Integration Chinese and Western Medicine with Nanjing University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (retrospective, n=411), an external test set from Yijishan Hospital of Wannan Medical College (retrospective, n=162), and a validation set (prospective, n=67). Deep learning (DL) and handcrafted radiomics features were extracted separately from US images. After feature fusion, the features were Z-score normalized and selected using the Mann-Whitney U test or Chi-squared test, with Fisher's exact test used when appropriate, followed by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. A DL radiomics (DLR) model was developed based on 10 machine learning algorithms and subsequently incorporated with independent clinical factors through logistic regression to build a DLRN. Model performance was evaluated by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration and decision curve, along with SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis for interpretability.
Logistic regression was selected as the optimal DLR algorithm, achieving AUCs of 0.90 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.87-0.93] in the training set, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.84-0.94) in the external test set, and 0.82 (95% CI: 0.71-0.91) in the prospective validation set. The DLRN, refined by integrating independent clinical factors via logistic regression, demonstrated superior discrimination with AUCs of 0.93, 0.94, and 0.92 in the training, external test, and prospective validation sets, respectively. The DLRN model demonstrated robust clinical applicability, as evidenced by calibration and decision curve analyses. SHAP analysis enhanced DLRN interpretability by quantifying feature contributions to individual predictions and overall model output.
The DLRN model was designed for the preoperative identification of malignant TNs in LT, thereby facilitating personalized treatment.

title: A deep learning-based model combining quantitative parameters of initial chest computed tomography and clinical variables for the prediction of posttraumatic acute respiratory distress syndrome.
authors: Wenzhao Zhang; Xu Hu; Ke Ning; Huayan Xu; Jianqun Yu
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) frequently complicates severe trauma, and early risk stratification for this condition remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a combined prediction model integrating deep learning-based quantitative parameters of initial chest computed tomography (CT) with clinical variables for the early prediction of posttraumatic ARDS, with a focus on automation and interpretability for potential integration with emergency workflows.
A total of 173 patients with trauma admitted to West China Hospital of Sichuan University from January to June 2024 were retrospectively screened, and 105 patients were finally enrolled (34 in the ARDS group and 71 in the nonARDS group). Clinical data were collected, and quantitative parameters (e.g., opacity score, opacity volume, opacity percentage, highattenuation opacity volume, and mean CT value) were automatically extracted with deep learning-based CT quantitative analysis software. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with ARDS. The final multivariate model was expressed as follows: logit(ARDS risk) = -4.623 + [0.142 × Injury Severity Score (ISS)] + [0.247 × procalcitonin (PCT)] + (0.113 × bilateral lung opacity percentage). Model stability was evaluated via bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions), and the predictive performance was assessed according to the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves.
Compared with the non-ARDS group, the ARDS group had a higher ISS (40 vs. 25, P<0.001), lactate level (3.9 vs. 1.9 mmol/L, P<0.001), and PCT level (3.2 vs. 0.2 ng/mL, P<0.001), as well as a lower Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (12 vs. 15, P<0.001) and SpO2 (94.8% vs. 96.7%, P=0.038). The ARDS group also had a significantly higher bilateral lung opacity volume (186.3 vs. 56.7 mL, P=0.001), opacity percentage (5.2% vs. 1.8%, P=0.002), and high-attenuation opacity volume (45.8 vs. 9.0 mL, P=0.001). Multivariate analysis identified the independent predictors of ARDS to be ISS [odds ratio (OR) =1.15; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06-1.24; P<0.001], PCT (OR =1.28; 95% CI: 1.04-1.58; P=0.02), and bilateral lung opacity percentage (OR =1.12; 95% CI: 1.04-1.21; P=0.004). The combined model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.892 (95% CI: 0.832-0.952). At the optimal cutoff of 0.385, the sensitivity and specificity were 82.4% and 85.9%, respectively. Bootstrap internal validation confirmed good model stability (mean AUC =0.878; 95% CI: 0.821-0.934).
Quantitative parameters of initial chest CT within 24 hours after trauma, especially bilateral lung opacity percentage, are associated with the development of ARDS in patients with trauma and may serve as objective imaging biomarkers for early risk assessment. The prediction model combining ISS score and PCT with automated CT quantitative parameters demonstrated good discriminative ability (AUC =0.892) and clinical operability and can be automated within minutes in a research setting. Further implementation studies are needed before the model can be implemented after the initial CT scan in clinical settings; nonetheless, the model may serve as a decision support tool and as a component in implementing early lung-protective strategies.

title: A competition-proven deep learning-based dual-domain framework for low-dose CBCT reconstruction.
authors: Xuzhi Zhao; Muliang Li; Yi Du
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Low-dose cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging reduces radiation exposure but inevitably increases noise levels, leading to degradation of reconstructed image quality. This study proposes and systematically evaluates a deep learning-based dual-domain framework, named DLDF, for improving CBCT image quality. The effectiveness of DLDF is demonstrated by its first-place ranking in the low-dose task of the ICASSP-2024 3D-CBCT Challenge.
The proposed DLDF integrates a projection domain model (PDNet), based on a three-dimensional (3D) Res-UNet architecture, with an image domain model (IDNet), based on a two-dimensional (2D) Res-UNet architecture. Low-dose projections were first denoised by PDNet, followed by Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction, and then further refined by IDNet. The DLDF was trained on data from 800 patients, validated on 100 patients, and tested on 110 patients. On the validation set, the DLDF was compared with 10 state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning methods using five quantitative metrics: mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), feature similarity (FSIM), structural similarity (SSIM), and visual information fidelity (VIF). Statistical analysis was conducted using the Friedman test, followed by the post-hoc Durbin-Conover test with Holm-Bonferroni correction. On the test set, the DLDF was compared against 8 competing methods submitted by other participants.
The proposed DLDF preserved anatomical structures and fine details with notable improvements in overall visual integrity, while also demonstrating improved performance across quantitative metrics. On the validation set, the DLDF achieved average MSE, PSNR, FSIM, SSIM, and VIF values of 0.00162, 35.54 dB, 0.9709, 0.9186, and 0.8492, respectively, outperforming all 10 SOTA methods with statistically significant improvements across all metrics (P<0.05). On the test set, the DLDF achieved an average MSE of 0.00145, ranking first among all competing methods submitted by the participants.
The proposed DLDF effectively improves the quality of low-dose CBCT images. By enabling high-quality reconstructions from lower radiation exposures, this framework may help reduce patient dose and associated health risks in clinical CBCT applications. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Xuzhi-bjtu/ICASSP-2024-3D-CBCT-challenge-Low-dose-CBCT-reconstruction.

title: Deep learning-based segmentation, grading and genotype classification of glioma: a literature analysis.
authors: Weihan Song; Yuan Hu; Yi Wang; Jian Ruan; Bo Lin; Weibin Yang
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
Glioma represents the most prevalent and lethal primary brain tumor in adults, and its high mortality poses a significant challenge to clinical decision-making. While the conventional gold standard for diagnosis relies on the examination of surgically resected tumor tissue, recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, have demonstrated compelling performance in medical image analysis, offering the potential for non-invasive prediction of the genetic and histological features of glioma as well as automatic tumor segmentation. This review aims to comprehensively summarize deep learning-based techniques for glioma segmentation, grading, and genotype classification.
A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Xplore, and Scopus for articles published in English between January 2014 and December 2025, using combinations of the terms "glioma", "brain tumor", "deep learning", "convolutional neural network", "segmentation", "classification", "grading", "genotype", "isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)", "1p/19q", and "O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT)". Peer-reviewed studies that applied deep learning methods to glioma analysis using medical imaging data and reported quantitative performance results were included, whereas review articles without original results, studies using exclusively non-deep-learning methods, and studies focused solely on non-glioma brain tumors were excluded.
This review first summarizes the commonly used public datasets [Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS), The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), synthetic, and private cohorts] and performance metrics, and then surveys deep learning-based approaches for glioma segmentation, grading, and genotype classification according to task. Recent methodological advances, including Vision Transformers, foundation models such as the segment anything model (SAM) and MedSAM, diffusion models, and self-supervised learning, are also discussed. Reported performance varies considerably across datasets and evaluation protocols, and risks of bias, including slice-level data leakage, patient overlap across public repositories, and single-center confounding, remain prevalent in the genotype prediction literature.
Deep learning has become a transformative tool for non-invasive glioma characterization. Future research should prioritize prospective multi-center validation, standardized evaluation protocols, calibrated uncertainty estimation, and clinically deployable frameworks, thereby facilitating the translation of these techniques into routine diagnostic workflows and ultimately improving outcomes for patients with glioma.

title: Quantification of plaque and detection of high-risk plaque characteristics based on coronary computed tomography angiography: comparison between superresolution deep learning reconstruction and hybrid iterative reconstruction.
authors: Limiao Zou; Keting Xu; Xiaohuan Liu; Cheng Xu; Haipeng Liu; Ying Li; Ying Li; Tao Zhou; Lin Yang; Chunli Zhao; Na Li; Yi Lv; Wenli Hong; Bo Wang; Lijun Chen; Min Xu; Yufei Li; Yunxin Zhong; Zhiping Zhong; Jikun Zheng; Zhihua Wu; Hongzhong Mo; Tong Zhang; Demao Deng; Yaliang Liu; Shouqiang Jia; Shaofei He; Changhua Liang; Yining Wang
journal: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
abstract:
In addition to stenosis evaluation, coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) also allows for noninvasive plaque quantification and characterization, which informs risk stratification and management strategies. This study aimed to compare a novel superresolution deep learning reconstruction (SR-DLR) technique with a conventional hybrid iterative reconstruction (HIR) method in quantifying CCTA-derived plaque and detecting high-risk plaque (HRP) characteristics.
A total of 255 consecutive patients (mean age 63.7±9.6 years; 184 men and 71 women) who underwent clinically indicated CCTA for assessment of suspected or known coronary artery disease were prospectively enrolled. The HIR algorithm with the FC43 kernel and the SR-DLR algorithm with the cardiac kernel reconstructed the same raw CCTA data. Total plaque, calcified plaque, noncalcified plaque (NCP), and low-attenuation plaque (LAP) volumes were quantified. Moreover, the ability to detect HRP characteristics (LAP, spotty calcification, positive remodeling, and napkin-ring sign) was evaluated. Paired comparisons were made between the two reconstruction pipelines.
Compared with the HIR pipeline, the SR-DLR pipeline obtained higher median volumes of total plaque {103.4 [interquartile range (IQR) 52.9-201.7] vs. 124.5 (IQR 66.8-236.2) mm3}, NCP [43.9 (IQR 20.1-87.7) vs. 56.4 (IQR 25.2-115.7) mm3], and LAP [0.1 (IQR 0-3.0) vs. 0.9 (IQR 0-8.7) mm3] (all P<0.001); meanwhile, calcified plaque volume did not differ significantly between the pipelines [44.8 (IQR 16.2-100.6) vs. 44.8 (IQR 17.3-98.2) mm3; P=0.87]. SR-DLR detected more LAPs than did HIR (91 vs. 67; P=0.01), but there were no detected differences in spotty calcification (63 vs. 56; P=0.33), positive remodeling (110 vs. 110; P>0.99), or napkin-ring sign (42 vs. 40, P=0.76).
Compared with the HIR pipeline, the SR-DLR pipeline indicated higher total plaque, NCP, and LAP volumes, but no difference in calcified plaque volume was observed. Moreover, SR-DLR detected more LAPs than did HIR, while other HRP characteristics did not differ significantly. Further large-scale prospective studies including a reference standard are warranted to investigate the clinical impact of SR-DLR.

title: Opportunistic Cardiovascular Risk Assessment in the Eye Clinic: Validation of a Retinal Deep Learning-Based 10-Year Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Estimator.
authors: Simon Nusinovici; Heesuk Kim; Jaewon Seo; Tyler Hyungtaek Rim; Qingyu Chen; Zhiyong Lu; Chan Joo Lee; Yih-Chung Tham; Dongjin Nam; Sahil Thakur; Qingsheng Peng; Marco Yu; Geunyoung Lee; Sungha Park; Sung Soo Kim; Tien Yin Wong; Wathudurage De Silva; Tiarnan D L Keenan; Ching-Yu Cheng; Emily Y Chew
abstract:
To derive and validate a retinal 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk estimator ("Dr Noon cardiovascular disease [CVD]") and compare its performance with the clinical gold-standard pooled cohort equation (PCE) in a US population.
Prospective cohort study with up to 10 years of follow-up.
A total of 3096 participants (aged 55-75 years) from the multicenter Age-related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) with gradable baseline fundus photographs, including 1013 with PCE.
The Dr Noon CVD estimator, which incorporates a deep learning-derived retinal coronary artery calcium surrogate along with age and sex, was derived using a Cox proportional hazards model and validated within the AREDS cohort. Its predictive performance was compared directly with the PCE.
Incident fatal and nonfatal ASCVD events over 10 years. Performance metrics included risk stratification (hazard ratios [HRs]), discrimination (concordance index [C-index]), calibration (plot with intercept/slope), and reclassification (net reclassification index [NRI]).
Among 3096 participants, 202 (6.5%) experienced an ASCVD event. Although the PCE was precluded for 67.3% of the cohort (n = 2083) due to missing laboratory data, the retinal estimator provided scores for all participants with available imaging. Dr Noon CVD significantly stratified participants into low, moderate (HR, 1.84; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.24-2.71), and high-risk groups (HR, 2.54; 95% CI, 1.64-3.93; P-trend < 00.001). Beyond traditional risk factors, the model significantly improved discrimination (ΔC-index, 3.4%) and reclassification (overall NRI, 0.194; 95% CI, 0.044-0.344). In direct comparison among participants with PCE (n = 1013), Dr Noon CVD demonstrated numerically higher discrimination (C-index, 0.665 vs. 0.647; P = 0.74) and significantly superior calibration, whereas the PCE overestimated risk at higher deciles (P-intercept = 0.004 vs. 0.141 for Dr Noon CVD). Finally, performance was enhanced in hypertensive participants.
Deep learning analysis of routine retinal photographs provides cardiovascular risk stratification comparable to established clinical equations, offering a valid, noninvasive solution for opportunistic screening even when missing laboratory data precludes the standard risk calculators. These findings support the potential for opportunistic systemic risk assessment within the eye clinic, enhancing the role of the ophthalmologist in primary prevention.
